Times Square Ball Drop. An American New Year's Eve tradition centered in Manhattan, where a large illuminated crystal sphere descends from a pole at midnight on December thirty-first to mark the transition to a new year. The event has become a global symbol of Western New Year celebration, broadcast to hundreds of millions of viewers worldwide. Nearly a million people gather in Times Square annually to witness the sixty-second descent.

The ball has been dropped annually since nineteen hundred seven, making it one of the oldest continuous civic celebrations in America. The current ball, installed in two thousand eight, is made of two thousand six hundred eighty-eight Waterford crystal panels and weighs nearly twelve thousand pounds and is illuminated by thirty-two thousand two hundred fifty-six LED lights. The ball descends one hundred forty-one feet from its starting position atop a pole on the One Times Square building.

Midnight on the Eastern Time Zone is the official drop moment in the United States, establishing New Year for the country's televised celebration. The event is free to attend in person, with crowds gathering hours in advance in barriers that divide Times Square into viewing pens. Confetti cannons fire three thousand pounds of confetti as the ball touches the bottom, creating the iconic visual closure. The tradition began as a simple iron-and-wood ball in nineteen hundred seven, with periodic redesigns making it larger, brighter, and more elaborate.
